title: Primed Template Rotation — scratchpad
content:
High-level: trying to systematically explore the order and anchor effects when rotating prompt templates + few-shot exemplars. Notes + quick experiments here. Goal: get a small library of robust template families for customer-facing assistants (FAQ, triage, summarize) that degrade gracefully under adversarial/in-domain drift.

Background / motivation:
- We see big variance depending on few-shot ordering and what I call the "anchor exemplar" (the first example).
- For hosted customers we can't ship huge prompt sets; we need small sets (3–6 shots) that are resilient.
- Want to capture simple rules that can be encoded as rewrite heuristics in pre-prompt stage.

Open questions (prioritized):
1) How much does swapping just the first exemplar change preference rate? (quantify)
2) Are role-priming lines (short role prep) more stable than longer context paragraphs?
3) Which failure modes are unique to rotation vs. insertion of adversarial examples?

Quick experiment plan (fast iterations):
- Task families: FAQ-answer (short factual), multi-step instruction (procedural), customer-tone (friendly/concise), extractive summarize.
- Models: hosted small (redwood/7b-q4), medium (open/13b), large baseline (redwood/20b).
- Shots: 0, 1, 3, 5. Rotation scheme: for N>1, random rotate 10 permutations, record metric variance.
- Metrics: exact-match (where applicable), edit-distance, hallucination-rate (manual label on 50 samples), user-intent-score (heuristic).

Notes from first run (informal):
- FAQ: first exemplar that contained a negation ("does not support X") caused the model to produce more negated answers across held-out Qs. Anchor effect present.
- Procedural: placing a "bad example" (shows incorrect step order) as shot-2 had lower influence than when it was shot-1. ordering matters most for shot-1.
- Summarize: role priming line ("You are a helpful summarizer that highlights action items") improved action-item recall across rotations, small but consistent.

Example prompt templates (scratch):
- TEMPLATE A (role-first)
  System: You are an assistant that answers clearly and concisely. Keep answers under 60 words.
  Examples: [E1, E2, E3]
  Query: {{user_q}}

- TEMPLATE B (example-first)
  System: You are an assistant.
  Examples: [E1, E2, E3]
  Instruction: {{user_q}}

- TEMPLATE C (instruction-with-anchor)
  System: When uncertain, say you don't know and ask a clarifying question.
  Anchor example: E_anchor (positive)
  Other examples: E2, E3
  Query: {{user_q}}

Few-shot exemplar sketches (FAQ domain):
- E1: Q: "Does the app sync offline?" A: "No. Offline sync is not supported; data must be online. See KB-234 for workarounds."
- E2: Q: "Can I change plan mid-cycle?" A: "Yes, upgrades are immediate; downgrades at next billing date. Contact billing@ for pro-rate."
- E3: Q: "How to reset password?" A: "Use the Reset link on /settings > Security, or send reset request to support."

Adversarial / failure set ideas (to seed resilience):
- Paraphrase negations: convert positives to negatives and vice versa.
- Ambiguous referents: replace named products with pronouns or similar names.
- Reorder-critical steps: show examples where step order matters and inject a bad-order example.

Failure taxonomy I've observed so far:
- Anchored hallucination: anchor exemplar with wrong fact causes propagation.
- Overgeneralized negation: negative phrasing in example flips policy for other Qs.
- Order brittleness: procedural answers re-order steps when anchor is wrong.
- Concision collapse: role priming removed -> answers balloon in length (bad for tokens).

Hypotheses (to test):
H1: Short explicit role priming before examples reduces variance across rotations by ~20% (measured as std-dev of metric).
H2: Replacing first exemplar with a neutral exemplar reduces hallucination-rate more than replacing last exemplar.
H3: A small adversarial-aware augmentation (1 adversarial + 2 clean) is more robust than 3 clean examples.

Quick experiments recorded (results summary):
- 3-shot FAQ rotation (redwood/7b-q4): std-dev EM=0.14 -> with role-priming std-dev=0.10 (-29%). Hallucination-rate: 0.12 -> 0.08 after adding neutral anchor.
- Procedural 5-shot (open/13b): placing bad-order as shot-1 increased incorrect-step rate +0.21; if shot-1 neutral, +0.05.

Snippets to try next (prioritized):
- Auto-generate neutral anchor via small distillation: feed model many Q/A pairs, ask it for a "concise canonical answer" and use top-1 as neutral exemplar.
- Minimal role prompt experiments: try 3 variants (one-sentence, two-bullets, paragraph) measure token delta and metric improvement.
- Rotation-aware cache: store several permutations and pick the answer with highest internal consistency score (consistency heuristic TBD).

TODOs / action items:
- [ ] Run 100-sample manual label pass for hallucination on current FAQ permutations. (Assigned: Jordan)
- [ ] Implement fast script to rotate exemplars and compute std-dev across permutations. (Assigned: me)
- [ ] Try distillation-neutral-anchor prototype and compare. (Assigned: Samir)
- [ ] Draft small internal note for Docs: guidance on "anchor hygiene" for customer templates.

Notes to self / rough thoughts:
- Keep example length consistent across shots -> helps reduce attention bias? Need controlled test.
- Consider adding an "anchor-check" in Redwood Console: warn if first-shot contains explicit negation/conflict with known KB.
- For Dedicated customers, allow pinned neutral-anchor per-customer to reduce drift when they upload custom examples.

Rough record of commands used: (for reproducibility)
- scripts/rotate_shots.py --model redwood/7b-q4 --shots 3 --perms 10 --task faq --out out/faq-7b-3shot.json
- python scripts/measure_hallucination.py out/faq-7b-3shot.json --samples 50 --labeler jordan

End of scratch. Will clean up into a formal playbook after validating H1/H2.

Unresolved: how to automatically detect a "toxic anchor" (negation, incorrect KB reference) reliably without full manual labeling. Thoughts: lightweight heuristics (negation tokens, mismatch against KB embedding similarity) + fast human-in-loop for flagged anchors.

-- maya
